The UK Visas and Immigration agency has urged foreign nationals applying for its visas to watch for four warning signs that signal potential fraud. UKVI gave the warning in an advisory posted on its X handle on Wednesday, urging applicants to protect themselves from visa scams. “4 RED FLAGS to watch out for when applying for a UK visa. Protect yourself from visa fraud by learning these crucial warning signs in our infographic,” the agency said. The warning signs include people who guarantee applicants a UK visa or job, offer appointments or visa services that cannot be verified through official channels, and make unexpected contact to request money or personal information. The agency’s guidance also cautioned applicants against individuals who pressure them to act immediately or demand secrecy, describing such tactics as common signs of fraud. It said fraudsters sometimes pose as Home Office officials or representatives of visa application centres, offering services such as securing jobs, arranging appointments or processing visa applications. Some may claim there is a problem with an applicant’s visa and demand urgent payment to prevent cancellation or deportation. Visa fraud remains a major concern, with unsuspecting applicants often falling victim to scammers. UKVI warned that fraudsters could also use official-sounding language and forged documents, including seemingly genuine job offer letters, to convince victims. The agency said applicants should be wary of agents who promise to speed up visa applications in exchange for payments into personal bank accounts. “Visa officers will never ask you for money in person, by email or phone,” the guidance stated. It added that anyone applying for a UK visa or permission to travel would never be asked to pay visa fees through email, at a visa application centre or into a personal bank account. The agency advised applicants to make appointments through the official UK government website or its authorised commercial partner. It also warned that using forged documents could lead to visa refusal and a 10-year ban on applying for a UK visa. UKVI urged applicants who suspect fraud not to disclose personal information, hand over their passports or send money, gift cards or vouchers to suspected scammers. It advised people in the UK to report suspected fraud to Report Fraud, while those outside the country should contact their local authorities.
